title: Minimum Processing Time
statement:
There are `n` processors with 4 cores each, and exactly `4 * n` tasks. Processor `i` becomes free at time `processorTime[i]`, and task `j` needs `tasks[j]` units of time to run.

Hand every task to its own core, so each core runs exactly one task. A core starts its task the moment its processor becomes free, and cores never wait for each other, so a task `j` placed on processor `i` is done at time `processorTime[i] + tasks[j]`.

Choose the assignment that makes the last task finish as early as possible, and return that finishing time.
notes:
## Intuition

Only the slowest task on each processor matters, and a processor's tasks all start together. The finishing time is the largest `processorTime[i] + task` over all pairs, so the goal is to keep big tasks away from late processors. Trying every assignment is hopeless, but an exchange argument settles it: if a later processor held a longer task than an earlier one, swapping the two never makes anything finish later. So the earliest processor should take the 4 longest tasks, the next one the next 4, and so on.

## Approach

1. Sort the processors by free time, earliest first, into `processors`.
2. Sort the tasks by length, longest first, into `jobs`.
3. Processor `i` gets `jobs[4 * i]` to `jobs[4 * i + 3]`; the first of those, `longest`, is its slowest task.
4. Its finishing time is `processors[i] + longest`; keep the largest such `done` in `finish`.
5. Return `finish`.

## Example 1, step by step

`processors = [8, 10]` and `jobs = [8, 7, 5, 4, 3, 2, 2, 1]`. Processor 0 (free at 8) takes `8, 7, 5, 4`, so `done = 8 + 8 = 16` and `finish = 16`. Processor 1 (free at 10) takes `3, 2, 2, 1`, so `done = 10 + 3 = 13`, which does not beat 16. The answer is `16`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): the two sorts dominate; the scan touches one task per processor.
- Space: O(n) for the sorted copies.

## Pitfalls

- Sort the two arrays in opposite directions; sorting both ascending pairs the longest tasks with the latest processor.
- Only the first task of each group of 4 needs checking, because the group is sorted longest first.
- Use a numeric comparator: the default `sort` compares values as text, so `10` would come before `9`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `processors` | free times, earliest first |
| `jobs` | task lengths, longest first |
| `i` | index of the current processor |
| `longest` | slowest task given to processor `i` |
| `done` | when processor `i` finishes its tasks |
| `finish` | latest finishing time so far, the answer |

narration.2: Copy and sort the free times so the earliest processor comes first.
narration.3: Copy and sort the tasks longest first, the opposite order.
narration.4: Nothing has finished yet, so the latest finishing time starts at 0.
narration.6: Visit the processors from earliest to latest.
narration.7: Processor i takes the next block of 4 tasks; the first one in the block is its longest.
narration.8: Its slowest task decides when this processor is done.
narration.9: Is this processor done later than every one seen so far?
narration.10: Yes: it becomes the new overall finishing time.
narration.13: The last processor to finish sets the answer.
